bio.en: Drew Houston is co-founder and CEO of Dropbox, which he's built over 18 years through three eras—hypergrowth, attacks from Big Tech incumbents, and a painful reinvention toward productivity.
bio.zh: Drew Houston 是 Dropbox 联合创始人兼 CEO，18 年来他将公司经历了三个时代——超高速增长、来自科技巨头的围剿，以及痛苦地向生产力方向重塑。

summary.en: Drew reflects on Dropbox's three eras: early 10x hypergrowth, then near-death competition as Apple, Microsoft, and Google launched rival products (Google Photos' free storage “nuked” their model), and a forced pivot to productivity. He shares the emotional toll—employees not wanting to wear the shirt, the narrative flipping—and the lessons of resilience and reinvention under existential threat. The conversation is a candid founder's story of surviving platform shifts and staying alive.
summary.zh: Drew 回顾了 Dropbox 的三个时代：早期十倍超增长，接着是苹果、微软、谷歌推出竞品带来的濒死竞争（Google Photos 的免费存储“核平”了他们的模式），以及被迫向生产力转型。他分享了其中的情感代价——员工不愿穿公司 T 恤、叙事反转——以及在生存威胁下韧性与重塑的教训。对话是一位创始人坦诚讲述如何在平台变迁中存活下来。

turns.speaker: Lenny

And just that there were these weird dissonant experiences where salespeople just suddenly have problems selling into accounts that used to be a slam dunk, or things that used to work just stop working. And this happens. Blackberry's, and Nokia's best sales years happened in the years after launching the iPhone. So these things don't actually change immediately. And so Andy labeled these moments strategic inflection points for a company, and I'm like, "Yeah. Then, we're definitely in a strategic inflection point." (00:25:40): But they were dealing with, "Oka., our whole business is memory. How do we deal with this competition?" And there's this little vignette where he and Gordon Moore, one of the other co-founders of Intel, said, "Hey, let's pretend we're consultants to ourselves. What would we do?" And what they immediately decided was, "Oh, well, we clearly get out of the memory business, and put all of our chips on this sketchy little microprocessor thing that was much smaller. But very high growth, and potentially big market." And then they're like, "Well, why don't we do that?" (00:26:10): Only problem with that is it's like Google saying, "Yeah. Let's get out of search, and go all in on Gmail, or something, or YouTube." So it just seemed insane. Andy cautions in the book that, "Look, most of the time CEOs want options. They want to hedge their bets, but what you really want to do in these strategic inflection points is go all in one thing." Or as Mark Twain put it, "Put all your eggs in one basket, and watch that basket." And I was like, "All right. This makes sense to me, but man, this is going to be painful." So we go away for 4th of July. I'm with my family in New Hampshire. I reread the book, I come back. All right. I'm like, "Well, we really got to do it." Then, I just killed Carousel, killed Mailbox. Went all in on productivity...
turns.zh: 是的。我是罗杰的超级粉丝。我当时想，“好吧。好吧，如果我们认为我们在销售商品，那就尝试真正销售纸巾。” AG、宝洁公司以及许多消费品公司就是这么做的。而AG当时是宝洁公司的首席执行官。基本上，他和罗杰下载了他们如何看待竞争、市场和优势。其中很多都在认真思考你在哪里玩，以及如何获胜？ (00:23:28)：因此，对您所在的市场非常有选择性，并且只在您可以拥有领导地位的市场中。然后，明确说明您的领导地位是什么？因此，这是一件非常及时的事情，“好吧。Dropbox 看起来像一个产品，但它实际上参与了许多不同的市场。我们的最大风险可能是，我们在每个市场中都是第二名，这将是一个糟糕的情况。” (00:23:55)：另一本真正有影响力的书是安迪·格罗夫的《只有偏执狂才能生存》，我一直是安迪的忠实粉丝。高产出管理是他的另一本伟大的书，这是我对管理的介绍。至少，他的管理理论。所以很喜欢那本书。然后只有偏执狂才能生存谈论英特尔的经历，他们实际上发生了我不知道的事情，我们都知道英特尔是微处理器公司，Intel Inside。至少在80、90年代是这样。 (00:24:27)：但之前，它们是在微处理器中。他们出售内存、RAM。在 70 年代，他们遇到了这样的情况：他们是真正高增长、成功的内存销售企业。但当时，他们的日本竞争对手只是在更快、更好、更便宜地构建内存。就在每个维度上。还有可能是政府可能补贴这些制造商的反竞争行为。这种感觉不仅是他们在比赛中可能表现得更好，而且还没有一个公平的竞争环境。 (00:25:05)：但与此同时，你不会在他们的数字中看到这一点。他们还在成长。只是有一些奇怪的、不和谐的经历，销售人员突然在向曾经成功的客户销售产品时遇到问题，或者过去有效的东西突然失效了。这发生了。黑莓和诺基亚的最佳销售年份发生在推出 iPhone 后的几年。所以这些事情实际上并不会立即改变。因此，安迪将这些时刻标记为公司的战略拐点，我说，“是的。那么，我们肯定处于战略拐点。” (00:25:40)：但是他们正在处理，“好吧，我们的全部业务就是内存。我们如何应对这种竞争？”在这个小插曲中，他和英特尔的另一位联合创始人戈登摩尔说：“嘿，让我们假设我们是自己的顾问。我们会怎么做？”他们立即做出的决定是，“哦，好吧，我们显然退出了内存业务，并将所有芯片放在这个粗略的小型微处理器上，它要小得多。但增长速度非常快，并且潜在的市场很大。”然后他们会说，“好吧，我们为什么不这样做呢？” (00:26:10)：唯一的问题是，它就像 Google 说的那样：“是的。让我们放弃搜索，全力投入 Gmail 或其他东西或 YouTube。”所以这看起来很疯狂。安迪在书中警告说，“听着，大多数时候首席执行官都想要选择。他们想要对冲自己的赌注，但在这些战略拐点上你真正想做的是全力以赴做一件事。”或者正如马克·吐温所说，“把所有的鸡蛋放在一个篮子里，然后看好那个篮子。”我当时想，“好吧。这对我来说是有道理的，但是伙计，这会很痛苦。”所以我们7月4日离开。我和我的家人在新罕布什尔州。我又看了一遍书，回来了。好的。我想，“好吧，我们真的必须这么做。”然后，我就杀掉了Carousel，杀掉了Mailbox。全力以赴提高生产力...

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: Killed mailbox, went all in on productivity. To some extent, that was a relatively easy decision because most of our subscribers, 80% of people paying for Dropbox were using it at work. But that meant foreclosing on photo sharing and consumer and storage and all these things that Dropbox had become synonymous with and to this day are some of the things that we're most recognized for. And I wish I could say then everything got better. It was the opposite, actually, the narrative completely flipped on the company. The press started, we killed these new products, and then internally and externally, the narrative became super negative. Articles would come out every week or two, like, oh, Dropbox could be the first dead deck of corn. And then sometimes we've all seen this in tech companies get in this washing machine of self-perpetuating negative press. And if it goes deep enough, I mean, Uber had this for a while later, Meta's had this over their history, lots of companies where you just can't get the monkey off your back. (00:28:06): And then because what the reporters end up doing is they basically park their metaphorical van behind your office. They interview all the people that you just fired and then print everything that they say anonymously as if it were facts. And there's a lot of truth to what the press were saying, so I can't really blame them or saying they were being unfair, but it immediately put recruiting into this deep freeze. You're just in the situation. You've started this company, it's been super successful, and then suddenly your employees don't want to wear your T-shirt anymore. And frankly, you don't even want to wear your T-shirt anymore. It's just your pride in your own company takes a big hit. (00:28:50): And meanwhile, I've talked mostly about the external market competitive forces, but inside the company was a mess too. The business's revenue had scaled so much faster than our ability to hire and build the right infrastructure and operations internally. And so everybody's just panicking and being like, "All right, well good, Drew, we're not doing Carousel, we're not doing Mailbox. What are we doing?" And the truth was like, if I knew the answer to that, we would be doing it, but it's just this is going to take some time to figure out. So it was pretty tough when everybody's looking to you as the founder and CEO looking for quick fixes and answers, and also just wondering, how the hell did you get us in this situation?
turns.zh: 杀死邮箱，全力以赴提高生产力。从某种程度上来说，这是一个相对容易的决定，因为我们的大多数订阅者（80% 为 Dropbox 付费的人）都是在工作中使用它。但这意味着取消照片共享、消费和存储等所有这些功能，Dropbox 已成为这些功能的代名词，并且直到今天，它们仍然是我们最受认可的一些功能。我希望我能说一切都变得更好了。事实上，事实恰恰相反，公司的情况完全相反。媒体开始报道，我们扼杀了这些新产品，然后在内部和外部，叙述变得非常负面。每隔一两周就会出现一些文章，比如，哦，Dropbox 可能是第一批死掉的玉米。有时我们都看到科技公司陷入了自我延续的负面新闻洗衣机中。如果它足够深入的话，我的意思是，Uber 后来有一段时间也有这种情况，Meta 在他们的历史上也有这种情况，很多公司都让你无法摆脱猴子的困扰。 (00:28:06)：然后因为记者最终所做的就是他们基本上将他们的隐喻货车停在你的办公室后面。他们采访所有你刚刚解雇的人，然后匿名打印他们所说的一切，就好像它们是事实一样。媒体所说的有很多事实，所以我不能真正责怪他们或说他们不公平，但这立即使招聘陷入了深度冻结。你只是处于这种情况。您创办了这家公司，非常成功，然后突然您的员工不想再穿您的 T 恤了。坦白说，你甚至不想再穿你的 T 恤了。只是你对自己公司的自豪感受到了很大的打击。 (00:28:50)：同时，我讲的主要是外部市场竞争力量，但公司内部也很乱。该业务的收入增长速度远远快于我们在内部雇用和构建合适的基础设施和运营的能力。所以每个人都惊慌失措，然后说：“好吧，好吧，德鲁，我们不做 Carousel，我们不做 Mailbox。我们在做什么？”事实是，如果我知道答案，我们就会这样做，但这只是需要一些时间才能弄清楚。因此，当每个人都指望你作为创始人和首席执行官寻求快速解决方案和答案时，这是相当困难的，并且只是想知道，你到底是如何让我们陷入这种境地的？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So we're going to talk about how you're actually turning things around and the work you're doing now, learning from this experience. But I have a lot of questions about this part of the journey.
turns.zh: 哇。因此，我们将讨论您如何真正扭转局面，以及您现在正在做的工作，并从这次经验中学习。但我对这段旅程有很多疑问。

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to almost summarize the journey, it's like launch, killing it, viral, find all these opportunities, find all these big markets. You start three different product lines. There's the enterprise use case, there's the consumer file storage use case, there's photo sharing, there's productivity, and then basically every big incumbent's like, okay, great, we're going to come eat your lunch. And you end up fighting wars on three or four fronts against the big kahunas that have infinite cash and can do whatever they want. It's interesting the way you described the Apple launch of just like it was this mushroom cloud you didn't quite see for a while, but the Google Photos launch was like, okay, that was more clear of like, okay, this is bad news. I know it's always easy in hindsight of like, oh, I should have done something different when Apple launched this thing. But is there anything maybe you could have done, or was it even possible to have adjusted course at that point? Or was it like, okay, this is tough and we need time to figure it out?
turns.zh: 概括一下整个旅程，就像发布、杀死它、病毒式传播一样，找到所有这些机会，找到所有这些大市场。您开始了三个不同的产品线。有企业用例，有消费者文件存储用例，有照片共享，有生产力，然后基本上每个大的现任者都会说，好吧，太好了，我们要来吃你的午餐。最终你会在三四个战线上与那些拥有无限现金并且可以为所欲为的大魔王进行战争。有趣的是，你描述苹果发布的方式就像是你有一段时间没有看到的蘑菇云，但谷歌照片的发布就像，好吧，这更清楚，好吧，这是个坏消息。我知道事后看来总是很容易，哦，当苹果推出这个东西时，我应该做一些不同的事情。但有什么是你可以做的，或者甚至有可能在那时调整路线吗？或者是，好吧，这很困难，我们需要时间来解决这个问题？

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: Well, we panicked about the Apple thing too, because that also, that created a much smaller version of the tempest in a teapot that the Google Photos did. It was just much less public. Or it was just less obvious that we would be so out position. And actually we were more surprised to the upside when it's Google Drive launches, iCloud launches, OneDrive launches. And even as they build version two that we just didn't really notice that much of a problem. And I also studied over the years what happened in Netscape and companies like [inaudible 00:31:27] MySpace or these other cautionary tales. And interestingly, Internet Explorer was a thing that eventually undermined Netscape enough to permanently throw it into a negative trajectory. But Internet Explorer 1.0, 2.0, even maybe 3.0 just weren't that good and didn't really do anything but Internet Explorer 4.0, 5.0 and all the bundling, that really made a big difference, or big negative difference. (00:31:55): And then another thing that was interesting was, so there's a big time lag where between when these products launch and when they actually have an impact, because often it's not so much the existence of the product or it's availability, it's the constant bundling or the constant iteration, or it's the boa constrictor, in any given second, it's not much tighter, but over the following day, you're in a bad place. (00:32:24): But another thing that was interesting was one cool thing that we got to do and moving to California is you get to actually meet people who had been at these companies. And one of those people was a guy named Bill Campbell who was at Netscape during that whole period, and I had asked him, I'm like, "Man, that's really unfair. That sucks what happened with Microsoft and bundling with Windows and all these things and the antitrust and this and that." And he's looked at me, he laughed at and snorted and he's like, "Microsoft did not kill us. We killed ourselves." And so that was the other half of what was the problem within Dropbox was a lot of our wounds were self-inflicted in that we were struggling to keep scaling and launching all these products. And the Dropbox products had stagnated. (00:33:25): And I started to learn the hard way that, okay, yeah, I now understand what Bill is talking about, because we were hiring all these smart people, but the things we would do as a company would seem really stupid. And then some of these things were me personally, like yeah, I knew about from reading all these different things, but for whatever reason, I guess we just kept going anyhow. We were just too confident in our ability to respond, or we got lulled into this complacency, we were like, " Oh, well." Because it hasn't been a problem, it won't be a problem in the future. (00:34:03): But I'd say there's something about the Google Photos launch that just really set things off kilter. And then also for me personally, I think, I'd go from feeling good but stressed out all the time to mostly feeling bad all the time. And I just remember leaving, really trying to get away from the office for a little bit during this period, picked my teeth up off the ground. And the good news, I bought a place in Hawaii, so I was doing that in Hawaii, but didn't feel very good in any way. (00:34:42): And then I learned. I had to really figure out a lot of different things for myself to be the leader that could get us through this. Because mostly what I felt was like, man, I felt like we'd been doing such a good job, but now, man, if I really screw this up, or maybe I don't know what I'm doing. And then I had to really reset on a number of fronts. One is I just remember thinking my 18-year-old self would be like, what the hell are you complaining about? You did it. This is so great, and yet I felt so bad about things. And so I'm like, yeah, both of those things are true. How do I navigate that? And I think one part that was really helpful is getting a sense of equanimity basically, and doing a lot around mindfulness and meditation to distance... One thing that happens when you're a founder and your company succeeds is your identity is fused with the company. And so it's easy to get into a situation where you only feel good if the company's... Or how you feel is how the company is doing, and you need to separate that a little bit. So what that looked like for me is recognizing, yeah, there's really not an easy button that keeps things up and to the right forever. And most of the entrepreneurs that are my heroes had various periods of wandering in the desert. Those things instead of just being problems were probably the crucible that forged the people that they became. So the presence of badness is not necessarily you are bad. And it's like, yeah, now you're just getting your stripes as an entrepreneur. (00:36:41): And people were really helpful during that period. So I mentioned Bill Campbell. He was nice enough that we just stayed in touch and he would take me out to dinner every now and then. And I would be freaking out, but I was always surprised he'd never seemed to be freaking out. And mostly he'd just be saying like, all right, he'd dust you off and smack you and say, get your ass back out there. And he was literally a coach of the Columbia football team in addition to being a great technology executive and advisor to many of the great founders that I looked up to. He was really helpful because he helped me believe in myself even when I wouldn't believe in myself. And then people like Andy Grove who had written all these books, I'm like, well, at least I'm having this problem. But yeah, then that raised a question for me. I'm like, okay, I've been through this chapter one where everything's up and to the right, but I ran out of merit badges or Xbox achievements to collect. I was like, we did it. We got the product to this many users, we got it to where we got this valuation, or let me back up. So my whole life, or it's common, I think for a lot of founders, especially if you get good grades and stuff, you follow pretty linear path from childhood, from first get the right test scores, then get into the right college, get into the right college, take the right classes, get the right internship, get the right job. And early startup life is like that a lot. It's like, okay, have an idea. Find a co-founder, get into Y Combinator, get funding from Sequoia. (00:38:22): Watch an MVP just in 10 million, a hundred million, billion valuation. And I felt like we'd cleared all that. And so actually one of the other problems was, I don't even know what Dropbox needs to be and I don't even know what I need that I want to be in the world. And so part of this was also reconnecting to some kind of sense of purpose, because if I was really honest with myself, I was like, well, I'm just checking boxes and advancing and leveling up like a video game or something, but now I'm here. I'm like, all right, is it just big numbers bigger? It's also not that fun to just launch something that you put your soul into and then just have it get crushed with these competitors. It's even worse when you're bringing all these hundred other people who worked on that thing through that meat grinder too. (00:39:10): So are we just inventing things 10 minutes before Google and Apple do? If not, what are we doing? And then if we're really, really honest with ourselves, I think it's hard to argue that no one would've invented cloud photo gallery that wasn't constrained to your local storage. So I had to really rethink what does the company need to do. That actually took a longer time to answer than I wanted, but then also just what do I want to do? And I was like, well, you know what? I'm going to do this. (00:39:45): What I ended up settling on was like, look, coming back to my 18-year-old self, I was like, all right, stop complaining. This is a pretty good situation. You wanted something where the learning curve would be steep. Here it is. You get to do this really meaningful work to build things for millions of people, work with awesome teammates. There's always good things about it, and you've chosen this life, so stop complaining about the burdens because it's really dangerous if you start to resent the job or feel like a victim because that's just corrosive to everything else that you can get in this spin cycle.
turns.zh:
好吧，我们也对苹果的事情感到恐慌，因为这也创造了一个比谷歌照片小得多的茶壶里的暴风雨。只是公开程度要低得多。或者说我们的处境不太明显。事实上，当 Google Drive 发布、iCloud 发布、OneDrive 发布时，我们对它的优势更加惊讶。即使他们构建了第二版，我们也没有真正注意到那么大的问题。多年来我还研究了 Netscape 和 [听不清 00:31:27] MySpace 等公司或其他警示故事中发生的事情。有趣的是，Internet Explorer 最终对 Netscape 造成了巨大的损害，使其永久陷入负面轨道。但 Internet Explorer 1.0、2.0，甚至可能是 3.0 只是没有那么好，除了 Internet Explorer 4.0、5.0 和所有捆绑产品之外，没有真正做任何事情，这确实产生了很大的差异，或者说很大的负面差异。 (00:31:55)：另一件有趣的事情是，这些产品推出和真正产生影响之间存在很大的时间滞后，因为通常不是产品的存在或可用性，而是不断的捆绑或不断的迭代，或者是蟒蛇，在任何给定的时刻，它并没有更紧，但在第二天，你的处境就很糟糕。 (00:32:24)：但另一件有趣的事情是我们必须要做的一件很酷的事情，搬到加州后你可以真正见到曾经在这些公司工作过的人。其中一个名叫比尔·坎贝尔（Bill Campbell）的人在那段时间一直在 Netscape，我问他，我想，“伙计，这真的不公平。微软发生的事情以及与 Windows 捆绑在一起的所有这些事情以及反垄断等等，这真是太糟糕了。”他看着我，嘲笑我，哼了一声，他说，“微软没有杀了我们。我们自杀了。”这就是 Dropbox 内部问题的另一半，我们的很多伤害都是自己造成的，因为我们正在努力继续扩展和推出所有这些产品。 Dropbox 产品也停滞不前。 (00:33:25)：我开始经历惨痛的教训，好吧，是的，我现在明白比尔在说什么了，因为我们雇佣了所有这些聪明的人，但作为一家公司我们要做的事情看起来真的很愚蠢。其中一些事情是我个人的，是的，我通过阅读所有这些不同的事情而知道，但无论出于何种原因，我想我们无论如何都会继续前进。我们对自己的反应能力过于自信，或者我们陷入了这种自满情绪，我们就像，“哦，好吧。”因为以前不是问题，以后也不会是问题。 (00:34:03)：但我想说的是，Google Photos 的推出确实让事情变得不那么顺利。对于我个人来说，我想，我会从感觉良好但一直压力很大，变成一直感觉很糟糕。我只记得离开时，在这段时间里我真的很想离开办公室一会儿，把地上的牙齿捡起来。好消息是，我在夏威夷买了一个地方，所以我在夏威夷这样做，但感觉不太好。 (00:34:42)：然后我就学会了。我必须真正为自己想出很多不同的事情，才能成为能够帮助我们度过难关的领导者。因为我主要的感觉是，伙计，我觉得我们做得很好，但现在，伙计，如果我真的把事情搞砸了，或者也许我不知道自己在做什么。然后我必须在很多方面进行真正的重置。一是我只记得我18岁时的自己会是什么样子，你到底在抱怨什么？你做到了。这真是太棒了，但我却感觉很糟糕。所以我想，是的，这两件事都是真的。我该如何导航？我认为真正有用的部分是基本上获得一种平静感，并围绕正念和冥想做很多事情以保持距离……当你是创始人并且你的公司取得成功时，会发生的一件事是你的身份与公司融合在一起。因此，很容易陷入这样一种情况：只有当公司...或者你的感觉就是公司的表现时，你才会感觉良好，而你需要将其分开一点。所以对我来说，这就是认识到，是的，确实没有一个简单的按钮可以让事情永远保持正确。
大多数我心目中的英雄企业家都曾经历过不同时期的沙漠漂泊。这些事情不仅仅是问题，很可能是锻造他们成为这样的人的熔炉。所以坏的存在并不一定意味着你是坏的。就好像，是的，现在你刚刚获得了企业家的资格。 (00:36:41)：在那段时期人们真的很有帮助。所以我提到了比尔·坎贝尔。他很好，我们一直保持联系，他时不时带我出去吃饭。我会吓坏了，但我总是很惊讶他似乎从来没有吓坏过。大多数时候他只是说，好吧，他会掸掉你身上的灰尘，然后打你一巴掌，然后说，滚回去。他实际上是哥伦比亚橄榄球队的教练，同时也是一位出色的技术高管和我尊敬的许多伟大创始人的顾问。他真的很有帮助，因为即使我不相信自己，他也帮助我相信自己。然后像安迪·格罗夫这样写了所有这些书的人，我想，好吧，至少我遇到了这个问题。但是，是的，这给我提出了一个问题。我想，好吧，我已经完成了第一章，一切都正常，但我已经没有任何荣誉徽章或 Xbox 成就可供收集了。我当时想，我们做到了。我们把产品提供给了这么多用户，我们把它带到了我们得到这个估值的地方，或者让我支持一下。所以我的一生，或者说这是很常见的，我认为对于很多创始人来说，特别是如果你取得了好成绩之类的东西，你从童年起就遵循相当线性的道路，从首先获得正确的考试成绩，然后进入正确的大学，进入正确的大学，参加正确的课程，获得正确的实习，找到正确的工作。早期的创业生活也经常如此。就像，好吧，有一个想法。找到联合创始人，进入 Y Combinator，获得红杉资本的资金。 (00:38:22)：看看 MVP 的估值只有 1000 万、1 亿、10 亿。我觉得我们已经清除了所有这些。事实上，其他问题之一是，我什至不知道 Dropbox 需要什么，我什至不知道我想要进入这个世界需要什么。因此，其中一部分也是重新连接到某种目的感，因为如果我真的对自己诚实，我会想，好吧，我只是像电子游戏或其他东西一样勾选框并前进和升级，但现在我在这里。我想，好吧，只是数字更大吗？仅仅推出一些你投入了全部精力的东西，然后就被这些竞争对手压垮，这也不是那么有趣。更糟糕的是，当你把所有其他数百人也通过绞肉机从事这件事时，情况会更糟。 (00:39:10)：那么我们只是比谷歌和苹果早 10 分钟发明东西吗？如果没有，我们在做什么？然后，如果我们对自己真的非常诚实，我认为很难说没有人会发明不受本地存储​​限制的云照片库。所以我必须真正重新思考公司需要做什么。这实际上花了比我想要的更长的时间来回答，但我到底想做什么？我当时想，好吧，你知道吗？我要做这个。 (00:39:45)：我最终决定，看，回到 18 岁的自己，我想，好吧，别抱怨了。这是一个非常好的情况。你想要一些学习曲线陡峭的东西。这里是。你可以做这项真正有意义的工作，为数百万人构建东西，与优秀的队友一起工作。它总是有好的一面，而且你选择了这种生活，所以不要再抱怨负担了，因为如果你开始怨恨这份工作或感觉自己像个受害者，那真的很危险，因为这只会腐蚀你在这个旋转周期中所能得到的一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What helped you come to that place? Because that sounds like a very hard place to get to and a very important place. Was that Bill Campbell advice? How long did it take you to go from this is not going well and life sucks to, okay, let's look at it this way?
turns.zh: 是什么帮助你来到那个地方？因为那听起来像是一个非常难以到达的地方，但却是一个非常重要的地方。这是比尔·坎贝尔的建议吗？你花了多长时间才从不顺利、生活糟糕到“好吧，让我们这样看”？

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: I think there were a couple unlocks that were pretty fast, but I think again, this was not like, oh, then I felt better and we lived happily ever after at all. There were some moments of recognition where I was able to, I always try to get away from the mayhem or the whirlwind and recenter myself and do think weeks and things like that. And so those were really helpful because I felt when I diagnosed, well, when I'm on this treadmill and just firefighting or how did I miss this important thing? It's like, well, basically the root causes of being on the treadmills, I was too busy firing to aim, and then I thought I would do my aiming on vacations and things like that. But no, I need to get off the treadmill every now and then and make the space to really address some of these bigger questions. (00:41:31): Because it's not like I didn't forget about them. They just were always below the fold on my to-do list to deal with. And then until a few years go by and you're like, wait. Yeah, we really were just strategically out of position. The other way I came to some of these conclusions is a combination of things. So I think picking up a meditation or mindfulness practice, having therapists personally, having coaches, having friends and mentors, other founder friends. And so I wouldn't say it was any one thing, but I think you have to build this whole ecosystem of support around yourself and recognize no one's going to do that for you. And it's super important. (00:42:12): And then to Bill's other point, he was like, yeah, Microsoft wasn't killing us, we were killing ourselves, I think having to ask some hard questions to myself of, yeah, some of these wounds were self-inflicted. As much as there might be, I could look at this and say, oh, Microsoft is mean, or Google was mean, or Apple was mean, but I'm like, I drove the ship towards these rocks. So that's one downside of being founder, CEO. You can't blame the last guy. I think one of the big questions every founder has to figure out is not just, how do I have equanimity? What's my purpose? But then also, what am I doing that is destroying the company? (00:42:57): Because everybody's got strengths and weaknesses, but as CEO, both your strengths and your weaknesses are massively amplified and a lot of blind spots in your personality can become huge cultural dysfunctions in the company. And so step one to dealing with that is building awareness. And one thing that floated around the company for a while was the Enneagram, which on the surface is a personality typing thing like Myers-Briggs. I often describe it as it's like Myers-Briggs, but actually useful. The way it works is it's a personality typing system. You get a number from one through nine that's your dominant... Or there's nine types that are numbered. It's similar to Myers-Briggs in that Myers-Briggs has 16 types of letters like ENFJ or different things. But I find that Myers-Briggs is more descriptive. So it tells you, okay, you're an introvert, not an extrovert or vice versa. You're judging instead of perceiving. But I could never really work out what that meant. And so it's descriptive versus predictive or causal. (00:44:06): Enneagram I find is the theory that is really about your fundamental motivations. What are you running towards and what are you running away from? And the theory goes through some combination of your wiring from your genetics and your early childhood. Your autopilot is fixed after your childhood in that you just have instinctive responses to things. Now it's autopilot. It doesn't mean it's your destiny. You could override it, but it's super important to become aware of what are you running from and towards. And the Enneagram gives you a really good map to do that. (00:44:44): And so I'm reading this book and it starts by you type yourself, and I'm rolling my eyes. I'm like, okay, I'm a seven. What's a seven? And then you read, each type has its own chapter and you read the chapter and I was like, oh my God, this completely describes who I am down to my core. And I was almost looking over my shoulder. Who the hell did this? I thought I was a special snowflake, but apparently not. Okay, I'm listening. And [inaudible 00:45:16] with a lot of my early coaching experiences, which are, you do a 360, your coach sits you down, they're like, here are your strengths. In my case, it would be things like, oh, you're really creative and you like new ideas. That's okay. And second, you really love people. You build great relationships with people. I'm like, okay. Uh-huh. Third, you're really comfortable in chaos and resilient. I was like, this coaching thing is great. See, yeah, that was my first coach. And then you flip to your development areas because no one calls them weaknesses. (00:45:49): It's like, all right, one is you're bored by routine and really undisciplined. Second is you're really conflict avoidant. And third is you're intuitive, but you're also pretty chaotic and don't create enough structure for people so they're mostly confused. And when you pair the two together, you're like, oh, wait. Yeah, I'm creative and like new ideas, but I'm bored by routine and I'm a bit of a space cadet. All right, you love good relationships with people, but you don't want to make them unhappy so you don't tell them the truth basically about things that are difficult to hear. And it's going to be a similar map of things depending on your personality type or circumstances. But the Enneagram was that map for me to be like, okay, I've got these things that are genuinely great, but I need to address these downsides of the company's conflict avoidant, so we're not telling the truth and then making a bunch of predictable mistakes, or I'm creating this really chaotic environment where people don't know what they're supposed to be doing. (00:46:57): That's a problem. My personality is quite directly, I'm going to torpedo the company unless I do something about it. The same is true for any founder. And I'm a type seven, it's the enthusiast. It's like, again, central casting is like a lot of new things and creative and love just interesting things. But then a space cadet, FOMO, some of the shadow side of it, and every type has a thing like that. So really understanding, okay then, I was also just frustrated in the day-to-day of my work, I'm like, yeah, I'm not really getting to do these creative things where I'm too busy firing to aim. I'm missing these bigger picture things that are really taking the ship way too close to the rocks. Okay. Then I need to then understand what those things are and either work on myself or hire the right people who don't have those issues or one way or another, just make it so the company is not so exposed to my personal dysfunction. (00:47:56): And so yeah, it was a whole constellation of things like that where it's like, all right, we have to get... I mean, after this whole tailspin, we got to work. I'm like, all right, first business issues. The most urgent issues were just blowing all this cash. We need to get the P&L to look a lot better and get out of this land grab mode or fighting with Google on giving more free storage away or just being in these fundamentally unprofitable things. And so we did that. We cut the unprofitable parts of the business. We turned cash flow positive in 2016, maybe several months after this reckoning, and that set the tracks for getting into a billion run rate in 2017, going public in 2018. (00:48:40): We had to come up with a new vision and mission for the company, which I'll maybe save for chapter three. And then I was also just trying to do things that helped sustain me through the difficult things. I'm like, well, I am an engineer. As a little kid, I was coding since childhood. I knew I wanted be a founder. I didn't know I wanted be a CEO, so I backed into being a CEO. And then, so I'm like, man, there's a lot of tedious things about being an executive. So I was like, I'm going to find ways to automate tedious parts of my job and learn machine learning in 2016 and '17, and that ended up being really important later on. But then also it's just coming to terms with my job and what I wanted to do from a personal perspective, which included things like, oh, I'm lucky in that being a CEO is, I always wanted a steep learning curve. (00:49:33): In a lot of professions like in sports or math or chess or certain academic fields, you peak in your twenties or thirties. CEO's not like that. You can go your whole life and still not be a master. So I'm like, for better or worse, it's pretty cool that I can do this kind of work. And then I don't really get that much out of just chasing bigger numbers. The thing that is my favorite thing about Dropbox is looking over someone's shoulder in Starbucks and seeing if the little Dropbox icon is there. Building something that becomes a verb, taking some of the pain out of technology, things like that. So really reorienting. Yeah, it's not about just the external scoreboard just much. It's more about the craft of being a great CEO and building things I'm really proud of or really making a difference. And so those kinds of things, none of them all coalesce. It's like this lens that slowly and stubbornly comes into focus, but making the time to have some of that reflection was super important.
turns.zh:
我认为有几个解锁速度相当快，但我又想了想，这并不像，哦，然后我感觉好多了，我们从此过上了幸福的生活。有一些我能够认识到的时刻，我总是试图摆脱混乱或旋风，重新审视自己，并确实思考几周之类的事情。所以这些真的很有帮助，因为当我诊断时，我感觉，嗯，当我在跑步机上救火时，或者我怎么错过了这件重要的事情？这就像，嗯，基本上是在跑步机上的根本原因，我太忙于射击而无法瞄准，然后我想我应该在假期之类的事情上瞄准。但不，我需要时不时地离开跑步机，腾出空间来真正解决一些更大的问题。 (00:41:31)：因为我并不是没有忘记他们。它们总是位于我要处理的待办事项列表的下方。然后直到几年过去，你就会想，等等。是的，我们确实只是在战略上失位了。我得出其中一些结论的另一种方式是综合多种因素。所以我认为进行冥想或正念练习，有个人治疗师，有教练，有朋友和导师，还有其他创始人朋友。所以我不会说这是任何一件事，但我认为你必须围绕自己建立整个支持生态系统，并认识到没有人会为你做这件事。这非常重要。 (00:42:12)：然后对于比尔的另一点，他说，是的，微软没有杀死我们，我们正在自杀，我认为必须向自己问一些棘手的问题，是的，其中一些伤口是我们自己造成的。尽管有可能，我可以看着这个说，哦，微软很卑鄙，或者谷歌很卑鄙，或者苹果很卑鄙，但我想，我把船开向这些岩石。这就是身为创始人兼首席执行官的缺点之一。你不能责怪最后一个人。我认为每个创始人必须弄清楚的大问题之一不仅仅是，我如何保持平静？我的目的是什么？但话又说回来，我做了什么会毁掉公司的事情呢？ (00:42:57)：因为每个人都有优点和缺点，但作为首席执行官，你的优点和缺点都会被大大放大，你性格中的许多盲点可能会成为公司巨大的文化障碍。因此，解决这个问题的第一步就是建立意识。公司里流行了一段时间的九型人格，从表面上看，它是一种类似于迈尔斯-布里格斯的性格类型。我经常将其描述为类似于 Myers-Briggs，但实际上很有用。它的工作原理是它是一个个性打字系统。你会得到一个从一到九的数字，这是你的主导......或者有九种类型被编号。它与 Myers-Briggs 类似，Myers-Briggs 有 16 种字母，例如 ENFJ 或不同的东西。但我发现迈尔斯-布里格斯更具描述性。所以它告诉你，好吧，你是一个内向的人，而不是一个外向的人，反之亦然。你在判断而不是感知。但我永远无法真正理解这意味着什么。因此，它是描述性的，而不是预测性的或因果性的。 (00:44:06)：我发现九型人格是真正关于你的基本动机的理论。你在奔向什么，又在逃避什么？这个理论将你的遗传基因和你的童年时期的联系结合起来。你的自动驾驶仪在你童年之后就固定下来了，因为你对事物只有本能的反应。现在是自动驾驶。这并不意味着这是你的命运。你可以忽略它，但了解你正在逃避什么和奔向什么是非常重要的。九型人格为你提供了一张非常好的地图来做到这一点。 (00:44:44)：所以我正在读这本书，它从你自己打字开始，我翻白眼。我想，好吧，我是七岁。什么是七？然后你读到，每种类型都有自己的章节，当你读到这一章时，我就想，天哪，这完全描述了我的核心。我几乎要回头看。这到底是谁干的？我以为我是一片特别的雪花，但显然不是。好的，我在听。 [听不清 00:45:16] 我早期的教练经验是，你做一个 360 度旋转，你的教练让你坐下，他们会说，这就是你的优势。就我而言，这会是这样的事情，哦，你真的很有创意，而且你喜欢新想法。没关系。
其次，你真的很爱别人。您与人们建立了良好的关系。我想，好吧。嗯嗯。第三，你在混乱中真的很舒服并且有弹性。我当时想，这种教练的事情很棒。看，是的，那是我的第一位教练。然后你转向你的发展领域，因为没有人称它们为弱点。 (00:45:49)：好吧，一是你对例行公事感到厌倦，而且真的没有纪律。其次，你真的很回避冲突。第三，你很直观，但你也很混乱，没有为人们创建足够的结构，所以他们大多感到困惑。当你将两者配对时，你会想，哦，等等。是的，我很有创造力，喜欢新想法，但我对循规蹈矩感到厌倦，而且我有点像一名太空学员。好吧，你喜欢与人建立良好的关系，但你不想让他们不高兴，所以你基本上不会告诉他们一些难以听到的事情的真相。根据你的性格类型或环境，这将是一个类似的事物地图。但九型人格对我来说是一张地图，好吧，我已经拥有了这些真正很棒的东西，但我需要解决公司避免冲突的缺点，所以我们不会说实话，然后犯下一堆可预见的错误，或者我正在创造一个非常混乱的环境，人们不知道他们应该做什么。 (00:46:57)：这是一个问题。我的性格很直接，如果我不采取行动，我就会破坏公司。对于任何创始人来说都是如此。我是七类人，是狂热者。再说一遍，中央选角就像很多新事物，有创意，喜欢有趣的东西。但是太空学员，FOMO，它的一些阴影面，每种类型都有类似的事情。所以真的理解，好吧，我也只是在日常工作中感到沮丧，我想，是的，我并没有真正去做这些创造性的事情，因为我太忙于射击而无法瞄准。我错过了这些更宏观的事情，这些事情确实让船离岩石太近了。好的。然后我需要了解这些事情是什么，要么自己解决，要么雇用没有这些问题的合适人选，或者以某种方式，这样公司就不会那么容易受到我个人功能障碍的影响。 (00:47:56)：是的，这是一整套类似的事情，好吧，我们必须……我的意思是，在整个混乱之后，我们开始工作。我想，好吧，首先是业务问题。最紧迫的问题就是花掉所有这些现金。我们需要让损益表看起来更好，摆脱这种土地掠夺模式，或者与谷歌争夺更多免费存储空间，或者只是从事这些根本上无利可图的事情。所以我们就这么做了。我们削减了业务中不盈利的部分。我们在 2016 年（可能是在这次清算之后几个月）实现了正现金流，这为 2017 年进入 10 亿运行率、2018 年上市奠定了基础。 (00:48:40)：我们必须为公司提出新的愿景和使命，我可能会在第三章中对此进行阐述。然后我也只是尝试做一些能够帮助我度过困难的事情。我想，好吧，我是一名工程师。作为一个小孩子，我从小就开始编码。我知道我想成为一名创始人。我不知道自己想成为一名首席执行官，所以我选择了成为一名首席执行官。然后，我想，伙计，作为一名高管有很多乏味的事情。所以我想，我将在 2016 年和 17 年找到方法来自动化工作中乏味的部分并学习机器学习，这在后来变得非常重要。但从个人角度来看，这只是接受我的工作和我想做的事情，其中​​包括诸如，哦，我很幸运，作为一名首席执行官，我一直想要一个陡峭的学习曲线。 (00:49:33)：在很多职业中，比如体育、数学、国际象棋或某些学术领域，你的巅峰时期是二三十岁。 CEO不是这样的。你可以走一辈子，但仍然成不了大师。所以我想，无论好坏，我能做这种工作真是太酷了。然后，仅仅追求更大的数字我并没有真正得到那么多。关于 Dropbox，我最喜欢的一点是在星巴克里从某人的肩膀上看是否有 Dropbox 小图标。构建一些可以成为动词的东西，减轻技术带来的一些痛苦，诸如此类。
所以真的要重新定位。是的，这不仅仅是外部记分牌的问题。更多的是关于成为一名伟大首席执行官的技巧，以及打造令我真正引以为豪或真正有所作为的事物。所以这些事情，没有一个能够全部结合起来。就像这个镜头缓慢而顽固地聚焦一样，但花时间进行一些反思是非常重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So much of what you're describing makes me think about founder mode in a lot of different ways. One is your point about how you didn't have a lot of time to think about where things might be going and how the markets are shifting, and that has to happen, basically, no one else is going to do that if it's not you. Also, just this idea of how much of the solution was you understanding yourself better, reflecting on where you have strengths and weaknesses. Also, I'll mention, so before I had Brian Chesky on the podcast, I asked you, "What should I ask Brian?" And you asked me to ask him basically about founder mode, which was the first time I think you talked about it, and now it's like this whole thing. So you've been in the middle of all that for a long time. I guess just any thoughts on the importance of that and how you think about that as a founder?
turns.zh: 你所描述的很多内容让我从很多不同的角度思考创始人模式。一是你的观点是，你没有太多时间思考事情可能会走向何方以及市场如何变化，而这必须发生，基本上，如果不是你，没有其他人会这样做。另外，这个解决方案的想法是让你更好地了解自己，反思你的优势和劣势。另外，我要提一下，在我让布莱恩·切斯基加入播客之前，我问你，“我应该问布莱恩什么？”你让我问他关于创始人模式的问题，我认为这是你第一次谈论它，现在就像整个事情一样。所以你已经处于这一切之中很长一段时间了。我想您对这一点的重要性有什么想法吗？作为创始人，您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: So founder mode means a lot of things to a lot of people. So it's a bit of a Rorschach test, but I think parts of it that really resonate with me are, there's this evolution you go on as a founder where you don't know what you're doing and everything is new and unfamiliar. And then you're also very involved in all the details because there's no one else to be involved in the details. It's not like someone else is coding for you if you're just in your room at home. But then over time, you have to, there's this, Ben Horowitz calls it the Product-CEO Paradox, where the first way that companies die is from founders not letting go. And so you need to learn to scale yourself and hand off your responsibilities and operate at a higher level of abstraction. But then the second way that companies kill themselves is the founders get too far away. (00:52:23): And I felt like I had done that. That's a big part of the problem that led to a lot of this chaos at the end of chapter two, where I was like, oh, man, I'm on this treadmill. I'm doing stuff, but I'm clearly not setting the right direction. Or people are confused or it's not working, and I was too distant from the product. And then there's all kinds of issues you can get into as you hire an executive team and get that to function well. And so I think there's a debate to what extent founder mode is a mindset or a destination. To me, I think the destination part is pretty important. I think it's like after that learning journey, suddenly you have this conviction from actually knowing, from having lived experience and navigating a lot of these things where suddenly it's a lot clearer. (00:53:10): You don't have the same kind of confusion or learning curve problem. And then if you start out being too far leaned in, then you lean out too far. And I think a lot of that founder mode flip is when you're like, hey, this is not the company I want to be running. I need to be more involved. I need to stop making excuses. And basically, I also don't want to apologize or negotiate all the time for the kind of company that I want to be part of and run. So I had that too over time, maybe more towards a chapter three, some of those elements of... And I don't know if there's a way to get to this destination without some level of pain. Certainly the Elons and Steve Jobs of the world had big spans of wandering in the desert where they were not as cool as they are-
turns.zh: 所以创始人模式对很多人来说意义重大。所以这有点像罗夏墨迹测试，但我认为真正引起我共鸣的部分是，作为创始人，你会经历这种演变，你不知道自己在做什么，一切都是新的和陌生的。然后你也非常参与所有细节，因为没有其他人参与细节。如果您只是在家里的房间里，这并不像其他人正在为您编码。但随着时间的推移，你必须这样做，本·霍洛维茨（Ben Horowitz）称之为“产品-CEO悖论”，即公司死亡的第一个原因是创始人不放手。因此，您需要学会扩展自己并移交责任并在更高的抽象级别上进行操作。但公司自杀的第二种方式是创始人离得太远。 (00:52:23)：我觉得我已经做到了。这是导致第二章末尾出现很多混乱的问题的一个重要部分，我当时想，哦，伙计，我在跑步机上。我正在做一些事情，但显然我没有设定正确的方向。或者人们感到困惑，或者它不起作用，而我距离该产品太远了。当你雇佣一个管理团队并让其运作良好时，你可能会遇到各种各样的问题。因此，我认为创始人模式在多大程度上是一种心态或目的地存在争议。对我来说，我认为目的地部分非常重要。我认为这就像在学习之旅之后，突然间你有了这种信念，因为你真正了解了，从生活经验中获得了这种信念，并在很多这些事情上进行了导航，突然间它变得更加清晰了。 (00:53:10)：您不会遇到同样的困惑或学习曲线问题。然后，如果你一开始过于内倾，那么你就会过于外倾。我认为创始人模式的转变很大程度上是因为你会想，嘿，这不是我想经营的公司。我需要更多地参与。我需要停止找借口。基本上，我也不想一直为我想加入和经营的公司道歉或谈判。所以随着时间的推移，我也有了这个，也许更多的是第三章，其中一些元素……我不知道是否有一种方法可以在没有一定程度痛苦的情况下到达这个目的地。当然，世界上的埃隆斯和史蒂夫·乔布斯都曾在沙漠中徘徊过很长一段时间，在那里他们并不像现在那么酷——

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: ... spans of wandering in the desert where they were not as cool as they are today. The things they were doing weren't working, and they managed things very differently in that sort of post wandering phase. Suddenly had this level of conviction, and intuition that they might not have had before, or they sanded down some of their more counterproductive instincts. Again, there's a lot of surface area. (00:54:27): I don't know if anybody has a common definition of founder mode, but certainly that evolution, the way I think about is it is very difficult. One of the hardest things when you're running a company is that you're hiring all these execs who the only thing you know is they know a lot more about the subject matter than you do. What does it even mean to bring someone in, bring an exec who had managed a double-digit billion dollar P&L at Google, and what am I supposed to tell him how sales works or marketing? It's easy to be too leaned out there where you're not really setting a clear direction. Each founder is going to have their own things that are easy, things that are harder. Step one is being aware of them, and then being intentional about, how do I offset those things? Then you eventually get to a point where the learning curve flattens out. You actually do have some experience, and you can have a lot more conviction about what the company should do, and where you want it to go.
turns.zh: ...在沙漠中徘徊的时间，他们并不像今天那么酷。他们所做的事情并没有发挥作用，而且在那种徘徊后的阶段，他们的管理方式也非常不同。突然间他们有了以前可能没有的信念和直觉，或者他们磨掉了一些适得其反的本能。同样，有很大的表面积。 (00:54:27)：我不知道是否有人对创始人模式有一个共同的定义，但当然，我认为进化是非常困难的。当你经营一家公司时，最困难的事情之一就是你正在雇用所有这些高管，你唯一知道的是他们对主题的了解比你多得多。引入某人，引入一位曾在谷歌管理过数十亿美元损益的高管意味着什么？我应该告诉他销售或营销是如何运作的？当你没有真正设定明确的方向时，很容易变得过于专注。每个创始人都会有自己的容易的事情和困难的事情。第一步是意识到它们，然后有意识地思考，我如何抵消这些事情？然后你最终会达到学习曲线趋于平坦的程度。你实际上确实有一些经验，并且你可以对公司应该做什么以及你希望它走向何方有更多的信念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The way you described it to me, which has really stuck with me, is as a founder, as you said, you're in there leaning in, doing, on top of everything, micromanaging. Then you lead out, and hire execs that you think are smarter than you, and delegate more. Then it's like, "Oh, things aren't going great," and come right back into it.
turns.zh: 惊人的。你向我描述的方式让我印象深刻，正如你所说，作为一名创始人，你要在一切之上进行微观管理。然后你带头，聘请你认为比你更聪明的高管，并授权更多。然后就好像，“哦，事情进展不太顺利”，然后又回到正题。

turns.speaker: Drew Houston
turns.en: Yeah. Specifically, it's often well-intended or it's often even not conscious, but as you hire these execs, and then you also build up an HR function, you get coaches, and things like that, and then the things are not going well, one thing that can happen is you start collecting all this feedback. People are like, "Wait, if I can give Drew some negative feedback, then maybe I can displace some of the ..." It's sort of easy to get into a situation where you're sort of being my to-do list of problems, just weaknesses, and flaws I needed to work on was super long, way longer than anyone else's. On the one hand I'm like, "Yes, I am wholly accountable, and responsible for everything in the company as its CEO." That's not wrong. But you can end up just carrying too much of the water, so a lot of it ended up having to be this pushing back a bit. Be like, "All right, yes, there are things I need to work on, but that can't be an excuse for my execs to somehow evade accountability." (00:56:52): There's these sorts of systemic things that can creep in for sure. Then you get this feedback, and you're like, "Now, I'm doing all this behavior," or, "Now, I'm behaving in ways that I don't think are really right." Or I'm like, "Everything is just negotiated compromise with everyone on the roadmap or on how we behave or strategy." At some point you end up blowing that up as a founder, and that was certainly my experience.
turns.zh: 是的。具体来说，这通常是出于好意，甚至常常是无意识的，但当你雇佣这些高管，然后你还建立了人力资源职能，你得到了教练，诸如此类的事情，然后事情进展不顺利，可能发生的一件事就是你开始收集所有这些反馈。人们会说，“等等，如果我能给德鲁一些负面反馈，那么也许我可以取代一些……”很容易陷入这样一种情况：你是我的待办事项清单，里面列出了我的问题、弱点和缺陷，我需要解决的问题非常长，比其他人的要长得多。一方面，我会说：“是的，作为首席执行官，我对公司的一切负有全部责任。”这并没有错。但你最终可能会携带太多的水，所以很多水最终不得不向后推一点。就像，“好吧，是的，有些事情我需要做，但这不能成为我的高管以某种方式逃避责任的借口。” (00:56:52)：肯定会出现一些系统性的事情。然后你得到这样的反馈，你会说，“现在，我正在做所有这些行为”，或者，“现在，我的行为方式我认为并不真正正确。”或者我想，“一切都只是与路线图上的每个人协商妥协，或者我们的行为或策略。”在某些时候，作为创始人，你最终会毁掉它，这当然是我的经历。

turns.en: My playbook as an entrepreneur is to get really frustrated by something, and then try to solve that personally. I'll cover the team, and what direction we ended up choosing together. My first frustration was forgetting a thumb drive, and then wanting to never have that problem again. (00:59:03): But my second big frustration was like, "Man, this scaling this company was way harder than it should have been." Thank God I had people like Bill, Andy, friends, mentors to guide me along. A lot of people don't have access to that. But I feel like I could have written myself postcards that would've made this a little bit easier. Or, there are just some things that don't make sense about how you scale a company. There seem to be things that are really broken about the way we work in general. (00:59:40): As I was piecing through a lot of the challenges, I'm like, "All right, what should Dropbox do?" We should probably not do things that would've been invented by everybody else 10 minutes later. Where are the problems that are not solving themselves? One problem I felt like was not solving itself was this problem of being just on this treadmill where I'm like, "I'm working really hard. I'm in meetings all day, emails all night. Is this it?" (01:00:08): First of all problem, no complaints. But I'm like, "This is so weird. Yeah, I'm making huge strategic mistakes, because I'm too busy firing the aim, and I'm upset at myself about a lot of these things." But then I look left, look right, I'm like, "Wait, everybody is too busy firing the aim." Everybody is on the same treadmill. (01:00:28): I'm like, "This is bizarre. Who's winning here?" It's like if I was working hard, and the company is benefiting, then no problem. But I'm very busy, but I'm not really productive. I'm not putting in a lot of creative input. Then the company's not getting a lot of creative output. It just seems like lose, lose, lose all around. (01:00:50): I'm like, "Why are we on this treadmill?" We know from brain science that people are most happy, most productive, fulfilled, engaged, kind of everything you want, where we'd rattle off the same list, like when people are focused, when there's some kind of flow state, when they've had enough sleep, when they have a sense of purpose. We know all that. Yet we go to work, and it's like this cage fight of who's busiest, who's gotten the least sleep, who's most inbox zero. Then you look at the environment on our screens, now, especially after COVID, we live with that. (01:01:33): That's where we work. We don't work in an office, no matter what flavor of hybrid you are, you're working on a screen. COVID relocated us from offices to screens. You look what's on that screen, it's like, "Yeah, if you wanted to design a working environment that made it impossible to ever focus, ever get into a flow state, bombard you with just constant interruptions, distractions, and busy work, then yeah, you can squint and see me even before COVID, but definitely after. (01:01:59): But that people are like, "Yeah, I'm really not feeling great." I'm not feeling super engaged because half of my work is bullshit, the other half I'm just distracted to death. I'm like, "Why is this this? All right. Maybe Dropbox doesn't have to exist. Maybe we did the thing. Maybe I should go." Maybe I'm ready for the tech bro ascendancy. Maybe I should be flying cars, space, cancer, climate ...
turns.zh: 作为一名企业家，我的策略是对某件事感到非常沮丧，然后尝试亲自解决它。我将介绍团队以及我们最终共同选择的方向。我的第一个挫败感是忘记了拇指驱动器，然后希望再也不会遇到这个问题。 (00:59:03)：但我的第二个大挫败感是，“伙计，扩大公司规模比应有的困难得多。”感谢上帝，我有像比尔、安迪、朋友、导师这样的人来指导我。很多人无法访问它。但我觉得我可以给自己写明信片，这样会让事情变得更容易一些。或者，有些事情对于如何扩展公司规模来说是没有意义的。我们的工作方式似乎确实存在一些问题。 (00:59:40)：当我解决许多挑战时，我想，“好吧，Dropbox 应该做什么？”我们可能不应该做其他人十分钟后发明的事情。那些无法自行解决的问题在哪里？我觉得自己无法解决的一个问题是，当我在跑步机上工作时，我会想，“我工作真的很努力。我整天都在开会，整晚都在发电子邮件。是这样吗？” (01:00:08)：首先是问题，没有抱怨。但我想，“这太奇怪了。是的，我犯了巨大的战略错误，因为我太忙于瞄准，而且我对自己的很多事情感到不安。”但然后我向左看看，向右看看，我想，“等等，每个人都忙着瞄准。”每个人都在同一个跑步机上。 (01:00:28)：我想，“这很奇怪。谁赢了？”就好像如果我努力工作，公司受益的话，那就没问题了。但我很忙，但效率并不高。我没有投入很多创意投入。那么公司就不会获得大量的创意产出。似乎到处都输了、输了、输了。 (01:00:50)：我想，“我们为什么要在跑步机上？”我们从脑科学中知道，人们是最快乐的，最有生产力的，最满足的，最投入的，你想要的一切，我们会快速列出相同的清单，比如当人们集中注意力时，当存在某种心流状态时，当他们有足够的睡眠时，当他们有目标感时。我们知道这一切。然而我们去上班，就像一场笼子里的斗争，谁最忙，谁睡得最少，谁的收件箱最多为零。然后你看看我们屏幕上的环境，现在，尤其是在新冠疫情之后，我们已经忍受了。 (01:01:33)：这就是我们工作的地方。我们不在办公室工作，无论你是哪种类型的混合体，你都是在屏幕上工作。新冠疫情将我们从办公室转移到了屏幕上。你看看屏幕上的内容，就像是，“是的，如果你想设计一个工作环境，让你无法集中注意力、进入心流状态，让你不断受到干扰、分心和忙碌的工作轰炸，那么是的，你甚至可以在新冠疫情之前眯着眼睛看到我，但绝对是在新冠疫情之后。(01:01:59)：但人们会说，“是的，我真的感觉不太好。”我感觉不太投入，因为有一半的时间我的工作是废话，另一半我只是心烦意乱，我想，“这是为什么？好的。也许 Dropbox 不一定存在。也许我们做了那件事。也许我应该走。”也许我已经准备好迎接科技兄弟的崛起。也许我应该关注飞行汽车、太空、癌症、气候......

turns.en: Yeah, right. But then I would talk to people who were actually working on those things, and they were on the same treadmill. I interviewed this director of engineering at SpaceX. I was like, "Oh my God, you're actually going to Mars. This is so cool. How do you guys work together? How are you going to get to Mars?" He's like, "I don't really understand the question." (01:02:50): I'm like, "What tools do you use? How do you work together? How are we going to get to Mars?" The answer was basically, "We're going to get to Mars through a lot of emails, and a lot of files." I was like, "Oh, my God." Most of the time, we correctly think about technology as just like force multiplier, like the amplifier of our abilities. But from another perspective, we're only as good as organizations as our tools, or tools can become the limiting factor. It's really a problem when the mechanism through which we were getting work done has gone from being a force multiplier, and amplifier to a suppressor. We are the frogs in the boiling water where this kind happen one day at a time. (01:03:36): All the people working on those things, and there are many others, they're all dealing with the same issues of, "I can't focus my tools. I'm fighting with my tools." Somehow the tools went from helping us get the work done to becoming the work, as we layer. It went from 5 of them, to 10 of them, to 500 of them. (01:03:51): Yeah. I'm like, "All right. If Einstein were alive today, what would his day be like?" He would wake up. He'd have to delete a bunch of LinkedIn notifications. He'd get down to work, start writing equations, and then someone would Slack him, and interrupt him. Then he'd get back to work. Would we still understand relativity if Einstein were living in that kind of working environment? Probably not. (01:04:17): Even just visiting my dad at work when I was a kid, a lot of things were the same. He had a phone, a PC and an office, but he could turn his phone off. He got 5 emails a day, not 500. He would literally come home from work with a briefcase, put it down, and stop thinking about work. Then when he would be in the office, he could close the door, and actually get stuff done. (01:04:40): I'm not saying we should go back to the early 90's, but I'm saying it wasn't always like this. The whole frontier of productivity at the time felt like it was just taking us in the wrong direction. Things like Slack, which are wonderful tools, also chop up your day into little fragments, and make you cognitively diabetic. There's a lot of empty carbs in our collaboration, and our collaboration tools. (01:05:05): I'm like, "Okay, here is a problem that's not solving itself. Actually, none of our competitors even are framing the problem correctly. What we should be recognizing is that our ultimate non-renewable resource is our time, our attention, mostly our brain power, our creative energy. I think as a civilization, we're going to, hopefully in 5 or 10 years be like, "Man, we took this crazy detour where we basically hooked up that brain power to this thing that was just burning off half of it as friction with our tools." That was dumb. Yet no company was even talking about this, let alone fixing it. (01:05:49): Then we came up with a new Dropbox mission. It became Dropbox is designing a more enlightened way of working, because the way we were working is unenlightened, unexamined. Meanwhile, we were patient zero as the company. No one was doing a lot of thinking. Everybody's kind of busy. Everybody's bumping into each other. There were a lot of cultural problems. Like that we were faster. Your company grows, and rises, the easier it is for new people in the company to think they hit a home run instead of starting on third base. A lot of complacency, entitlement, and preoccupation with things other than our customers or other than our products set in. (01:06:37): It wasn't all bad. I think there were a lot of good things we had to pay attention to. We were scaling up the business financially. We were getting ready to go public. We had to mature a lot of things, but we lost sight of the place that money is coming from is from our customers, and the thing they really want is a great experience. (01:06:58): We've been tackling this in a lot of different ways. First is just things like after COVID hit, suddenly the world is working in a completely different way. We saw this as a big opportunity, not just a crisis. Or once you got past the crisis part of COVID, there was a big opportunity. COVID kind of wrecked everything, but we didn't have to put the floorboards back down in the same places. I'm a big fan of people like Peter Drucker, and lots of people who think about the nature of work, and this idea of we're finally decoupling work from our physical location. It's a big deal. It's probably one of the biggest changes to knowledge work in our lifetimes. Or even since Drucker coined that term knowledge work in 1959. (01:07:44): It's like, "Cool. For the first time, we can actually design how we work in ways that our parents couldn't, or the way that most of us just receive how we work from our parents." But like, "Hey, we can actually do things completely differently." We came up with this whole virtual first model where we're 90% remote, but then most importantly, we're trying to rebuild the new product stack for distributed work. I'll talk a little bit about where the new things we're doing, and then I'll come back to how we're rebooting some of the core. (01:08:16): But initially, after COVID, we studied a lot of how other remote first companies had worked. We synthesized with a lot of primary research of other companies like GitLab, Automattic, and others who had been doing this for a long time. We collated all that, synthesized a common playbook, open sourced it. If anybody's curious about this, you could find Dropbox. We've open sourced our virtual first toolkit. Then since COVID, designing a working model very in line with our new mission with a lot of benefits. It really works. The employee retention, satisfaction, engagement or offer separates all the things we care about have been significantly up since COVID. There's many factors to that, but there's a lot that's working about the model. But really, we're approaching it from a product standpoint. (01:09:07): In deciding to turn Dropbox into this lab for distributed work, we're like, "Okay, when you open up your laptop in 2025, 2030, what do you see?" Hopefully, there's some new stuff or some things that are different on there. What are those things, and how do we bring them back? (01:09:20): One of the first things you lose when you go distributed is context. We get a lot. You get a lot for free from osmosis. Just, "Oh, hey, how are you doing? How's this?" Or, "Oh, do you have that thing?" But then when you're remote, then a lot of that gets replaced with endless video meetings, and lots of Slack messages, which is super inefficient. (01:09:41): Also, one thing that was clear across the board from all the successful remote first companies was you have to be more documented, but then you have a lot more documents. This started turning up very obvious problems, which is like, "Wait, why do I have 1 search box at home, and 10 search boxes at work? Why is it easier to search all of human knowledge than my company's knowledge? Why is this problem getting worse not better every year?" If you think about it, we've got 10 search boxes that you search 10% of our stuff. I'm like, "We should just fix this." (01:10:14): Again, even just as a frustrated user, maybe 2018, 2019, I'm having this problem myself. I'm like, "It's really hard to find stuff." Plus there's always cool vector search stuff, and deep learning stuff happening. Even for ChatGPT, I'm going to make a personal search engine that takes us, so I shouldn't have to, right? If I search for strategy, and the title of the document is plan, it should get it right, and the matching should be fuzzy. Then I built something like this. I'm like, "Oh my God, it completely works."
turns.zh:
是的，对。但后来我会和那些真正在做这些事情的人交谈，他们在同一个跑步机上。我采访了这位 SpaceX 的工程总监。我当时想，“天哪，你们真的要去火星了。这太酷了。你们如何合作？你们要如何去火星？”他说：“我不太明白这个问题。” (01:02:50)：我想，“你们使用什么工具？你们如何合作？我们如何到达火星？”答案基本上是：“我们将通过大量电子邮件和大量文件到达火星。”我当时想，“哦，天哪。”大多数时候，我们正确地认为技术就像力量倍增器，就像我们能力的放大器。但从另一个角度来看，我们的组织取决于我们的工具，否则工具可能成为限制因素。当我们完成工作的机制从力量倍增器、放大器变成了抑制器时，这确实是一个问题。我们就像温水中的青蛙，这样的事情一天一天发生。 (01:03:36)：所有从事这些工作的人，还有很多其他人，他们都在处理同样的问题，“我无法集中我的工具。我正在与我的工具作斗争。”不知何故，随着我们分层，这些工具从帮助我们完成工作变成了工作。从 5 个，到 10 个，再到 500 个。 (01:03:51)：是的。我想，“好吧。如果爱因斯坦今天还活着，他的一天会是什么样的？”他会醒来的。他必须删除一堆 LinkedIn 通知。他会开始工作，开始写方程式，然后有人会放松他，并打断他。然后他就会回去工作。如果爱因斯坦生活在那样的工作环境中，我们还能理解相对论吗？可能不会。 (01:04:17)：即使只是小时候去上班的父亲那里，很多事情都是一样的。他有一部电话、一台电脑和一间办公室，但他可以关闭手机。他每天收到 5 封电子邮件，而不是 500 封。他实际上会提着公文包下班回家，放下它，不再思考工作。然后，当他进入办公室时，他可以关上门，真正完成工作。 (01:04:40)：我并不是说我们应该回到 90 年代初，但我是说情况并不总是这样。当时的整个生产力前沿感觉就像是把我们引向了错误的方向。像 Slack 这样很棒的工具，也会把你的一天分成小片段，让你患上认知糖尿病。我们的协作和协作工具中有很多空的碳水化合物。 (01:05:05)：我想，“好吧，这是一个无法自行解决的问题。实际上，我们的竞争对手都没有正确地描述这个问题。我们应该认识到，我们最终的不可再生资源是我们的时间、我们的注意力，主要是我们的脑力、我们的创造力。我认为，作为一个文明，希望在 5 或 10 年内，我们会像这样，“伙计，我们走了这条疯狂的弯路，我们基本上已经联系上了(01:05:49)：然后我们提出了一个新的 Dropbox 使命。它变成了 Dropbox 正在设计一种更加开明的工作方式，因为我们的工作方式是未经开明的、未经检验的。同时，我们作为公司是零耐心的。没有人做很多思考。每个人都有点忙。每个人都会遇到很多文化问题，比如我们的公司发展得更快，公司的新人更容易认为自己已经取得了成功，而不是从三垒开始。(01:06:37)：这并不都是坏事。我们在财务上扩大了业务规模。我们必须让很多事情变得成熟，但我们忽视了资金的来源是我们的客户，而他们真正想要的是一种很棒的体验。（01:06:58）：首先，就像新冠疫情爆发后，世界正在以一种完全不同的方式运作。
或者一旦你度过了新冠疫情的危机部分，就会有一个巨大的机会。新冠病毒有点破坏了一切，但我们不必把地板放回原来的地方。我是彼得·德鲁克（Peter Drucker）等人的忠实粉丝，也是许多思考工作本质的人，以及我们最终将工作与物理位置脱钩的想法。这是一件大事。这可能是我们一生中知识工作最大的变化之一。或者甚至自从德鲁克在 1959 年创造了“知识工作”这个术语以来。(01:07:44)：就像是，“酷。我们第一次真正可以以我们父母无法做到的方式设计我们的工作方式，或者我们大多数人从父母那里接受我们的工作方式。”但就像，“嘿，我们实际上可以完全不同地做事情。”我们提出了整个虚拟第一模型，其中 90% 是远程的，但最重要的是，我们正在尝试为分布式工作重建新的产品堆栈。我会谈谈我们正在做的新事情，然后我会回到我们如何重新启动一些核心。 (01:08:16)：但最初，在新冠疫情之后，我们研究了很多其他远程优先公司的运作方式。我们综合了 GitLab、Automattic 等其他公司的大量初步研究，以及其他长期从事这方面工作的公司。我们整理了所有这些，综合了一个通用的剧本，并将其开源。如果有人对此感到好奇，您可以找到 Dropbox。我们已经开源了我们的虚拟第一个工具包。自新冠疫情以来，设计了一个非常符合我们新使命的工作模型，并带来了很多好处。它确实有效。自新冠疫情以来，我们关心的所有员工保留率、满意度、敬业度或工作机会都显着上升。造成这种情况的因素有很多，但该模型还有很多工作要做。但实际上，我们是从产品的角度来处理这个问题的。 (01:09:07)：在决定将 Dropbox 变成这个用于分布式工作的实验室时，我们会说，“好吧，当你在 2025 年、2030 年打开你的笔记本电脑时，你会看到什么？”希望那里有一些新的东西或一些不同的东西。这些东西是什么？我们如何把它们带回来？ (01:09:20)：当你进行分布式时，你首先失去的东西之一就是上下文。我们得到很多。你可以通过渗透免费获得很多东西。只是，“哦，嘿，你好吗？怎么样？”或者，“哦，你有那个东西吗？”但当你处于远程状态时，很多事情就会被无休止的视频会议和大量的 Slack 消息所取代，这是非常低效的。 (01:09:41)：此外，所有成功的远程第一公司都清楚地看到一件事，那就是你必须有更多的文档，但随后你就有了更多的文档。这就开始出现非常明显的问题，比如，“等等，为什么我家里有 1 个搜索框，工作中有 10 个搜索框？为什么搜索所有人类知识比搜索公司的知识更容易？为什么这个问题每年都变得更糟而不是更好？”如果您想一想，我们有 10 个搜索框，您可以搜索我们 10% 的内容。我想，“我们应该解决这个问题。” (01:10:14)：同样，即使只是作为一个沮丧的用户，也许在 2018 年、2019 年，我自己也遇到了这个问题。我想，“找东西真的很难。”另外，总是有很酷的矢量搜索和深度学习的事情发生。即使对于 ChatGPT，我也会制作一个带我们的个人搜索引擎，所以我不必这样做，对吗？如果我搜索策略，并且文档的标题是计划，它应该是正确的，并且匹配应该是模糊的。然后我建立了这样的东西。我想，“天哪，它完全有效。”
